> The sea keeps no accounts, but it always collects.
>
> — saying of the Kervran fishing families

# The Weighing House

The weighing house at Port Aven had been closed for eleven years when Maëlle Kervran found the ledger. She had come for the scales — a buyer in Quimper wanted the brass beam, and her brother wanted the money — and she found the book instead, wrapped in oilcloth on the shelf above the counterweights, where no one had looked because no one had needed to.

It was heavier than it looked. The cover was sailcloth stretched over board, stiff with salt, and someone had written on the spine in white paint, long since cracked: *1961–1974*. She opened it standing up, in the grey light from the one unboarded window, and read the first line before she understood what it was.

*14 March 1961. Le Goff, Yann. Sardines, 212 kg. Paid 318 francs. Owed 40 to the house.*

Owed to the house. She turned the page, and the next, and the column on the right — the column of what was owed — grew longer with every week, the same names, the same boats, the debts carried forward in a hand that never changed.

"Maëlle?"

Her brother stood in the doorway, blocking the light. Erwan was forty-six and still stood like a man on deck, feet apart, waiting for the floor to move.

"The buyer's coming at four," he said. "Is the beam loose?"

"Not yet." She held up the ledger. "Did you know about this?"

He came in and looked at it without taking it from her, the way he looked at weather.

"Papa's," he said. "Or Grandpère's. Does it matter?"

"Look at the names."

He looked. She watched his eyes go down the page, and stop.

"Le Goff," he said. "Riou. Tanguy." A pause. "Kervran."

"Every family in the harbour," she said. "Every family owed the house. Every week."

"Everyone owed the house. That's how it worked. You sold your fish, the house took its share, you bought your ice and your nets on credit." He shrugged, but it was a careful shrug. "It's an old book, Maëlle."

"Then why was it hidden?"

He did not answer that. Outside, a gull landed on the roof and walked along the ridge, its feet loud on the slates.

---

The buyer from Quimper came at four and left at half past with the brass beam wrapped in blankets in the back of his van. Erwan counted the money twice on the bonnet of his car and put half of it into Maëlle's hand without a word, which was his way of apologising for something he had not admitted.

She drove home with the ledger on the passenger seat.

That evening she read it through, all of it, with a glass of cider she forgot to drink. The debts rose through the sixties, slowly, and then in the winter of 1968 they rose all at once: a bad season, she guessed, or a storm. By 1970 there were families who owed more than their boats were worth. And then, on a page near the end, the hand that had never changed wrote something that was not a number.

*11 November 1973. All debts of the Le Goff family transferred to E. Kervran, by agreement. Witnessed.*

E. Kervran. Her grandfather was Émile.

She sat back. The house was quiet; somewhere, the fridge hummed. *By agreement,* she thought. *Whose?*

# The Le Goffs

Yann Le Goff's granddaughter ran the bakery on the quay now, and Maëlle had bought bread there every Saturday for six years without once thinking about her name.

"Two *pains de campagne*," she said, "and — Gwen, do you have a minute?"

Gwen Le Goff looked at the queue behind her, then at Maëlle, then at the clock.

"After eleven," she said. "Come round the back."

At five past eleven Maëlle sat on an upturned crate in the yard behind the bakery, among flour sacks and the smell of yeast, and laid the ledger on her knees. Gwen lit a cigarette and did not sit down.

"My mother said you'd come one day," Gwen said. "Not you. A Kervran."

"You know about this?"

"I know my grandfather lost the *Santez Anna* in 1973. I know your grandfather got her a month later, and renamed her, and fished her for twenty years." Gwen blew smoke at the wall. "I know nobody in my family ever said his name at the table. I didn't know there was a book."

"It says the debts were transferred. By agreement."

"Does it say what was agreed?"

"No."

Gwen laughed — a short, unhappy sound. "Of course it doesn't."

* * *

That night Maëlle found the letter. It had been tucked into the back board of the ledger, behind the endpaper, and she found it only because the paper had come loose at one corner and she had tried to smooth it flat.

> *Émile —*
>
> *I sign because I have no choice and because you are the only one who offered. I do not forgive the house, and I do not forgive you for being the house. Keep the boat. Keep her well. When my grandchildren ask, I will tell them she sank.*
>
> *— Yann*

She read it three times. Then she put it back exactly where she had found it, closed the ledger, and sat for a long time in the dark kitchen, listening to the sea she could not see.

# Low Water

Erwan came on Sunday, as he did every Sunday, and found her at the table with the ledger open and the letter beside it.

"You told Gwen," he said. It was not a question; the harbour was small.

"I asked her. There's a difference."

"Not here, there isn't." He sat down heavily. He did not look at the letter. "What do you want, Maëlle? To give them the boat back? She was broken up in 1994. To give them money? Whose? Papa's dead, Grandpère's dead —"

"I want to know what happened."

"What happened is that a man owed more than he could pay, and another man paid it, and took the boat. That's what happens. That's what still happens, at the bank, every day."

"Then why did he hide it?"

Erwan was quiet for a long moment. When he spoke again, his voice was different — lower, careful, the voice of someone stepping onto ice.

"Because Grandpère was the one who weighed the fish," he said. "He kept the scales. He kept the book. He decided what everyone was paid." He looked at her at last. "Papa told me, once, when he was dying. He said the scales were never quite true. Not by much. A few kilos a week. For thirteen years."

The kitchen clock ticked. Outside, the tide was out; she could hear it in the silence, the absence of the sea against the wall.

"So the debts —" she said.

"Were ours," said Erwan. "All of them. From the beginning."

---

On Monday morning, before the bakery opened, Maëlle walked down to the quay with the ledger under her arm. The boats were in, the gulls were loud, and the light was the flat, pale light of low water, when everything the sea usually covers is suddenly, briefly, visible.

Gwen was unlocking the door. She saw the book and stopped.

"I think," Maëlle said, "we should read this together. All of it."
